body.heading: Ask about the ordinary, not the famous
paragraphs: “What was an ordinary Tuesday when you were twelve?” often unlocks more than “Tell me about the war” or “the old days.” Ordinary details — prices, songs, the walk to school, what was for tea — are the parts of history that vanish first and fascinate most.
Ask what they played, what they were afraid of, what made their parents laugh. You are collecting a person, not a timeline.

body.heading: Let the stories wander
paragraphs: Stories from older people travel by association, not by agenda. The detour about a neighbour’s goat may be the route to the best story of the afternoon. Resist editing; your only jobs are appetite and patience.
If they are willing, record the audio on a phone, with permission. Voices are the first thing families wish they had kept.

body.heading: Write down three things
paragraphs: Afterwards, write down just three things you heard — a name, a place, a phrase they used. Memory is a leaky bucket, but three written lines will hold a surprising amount of a person.
One day you may be the oldest library in the family. What you borrow now, carefully, is what there will be to lend.

takeaway: Ask about ordinary days, let stories wander, record the voice, and write down three things.
